meta_description: J. Press has dressed Ivy League men since 1902. Here's what's still made in the USA, what's not, and whether it's worth your money.
lead: The original Ivy League clothier, still making Oxford shirts and Shaggy Dog sweaters in the USA, 120-plus years on.

sections.verdict: Yes, though only if you're buying from the American site and checking the label. J. Press is a split operation: the U.S. line includes genuinely made-in-USA Oxford shirts and select knitwear at prices that hold up against any domestic competition, but the brand's Japanese arm is six times larger and largely Asia-manufactured, so "J. Press" alone doesn't tell you where your garment came from. Buy from jpressonline.com, confirm the origin on the product page, and you're getting real American goods from a brand that helped define American style. That's a worthwhile transaction.
sections.commitment: The American operation and the Japanese operation share a name, a history, and not much else. On jpressonline.com, the Oxford cloth button-down shirts are sewn in American workrooms, and a meaningful selection of knitwear carries a USA or Scotland origin. That's the good news. The less tidy news: Onward Holdings, the Japanese parent company since 1986, operates a J. Press business in Japan that is roughly six times the size of the American one, with a product line manufactured largely across Asia. If you buy J. Press from a Japanese retailer or a grey-market reseller, you may be buying something from that parallel universe. Stick to the American site, read the product page, and the brand's transparency on domestic goods is actually better than most, they call it out as a feature, not a footnote.
sections.character: J. Press didn't just sell to the Ivy League, it invented the way the Ivy League dressed. When Jacobi Press opened his tailoring shop at the edge of Yale's campus in 1902, he was building a wardrobe language: natural-shoulder sack suits, Oxford cloth button-downs, repp-stripe ties, Shetland wool sweaters. That language spread to Harvard Square, Manhattan, and Washington, D.C., and its customer list eventually included Cary Grant, Duke Ellington, and Robert Frost. The Shaggy Dog sweater, a hand-brushed crew-neck Shetland pullover in a staggering range of colors, is the brand's most iconic single garment and one of the most imitated pieces in American menswear. J. Press does not chase fashion. It embodies a conviction that the sack suit and the Oxford shirt are simply correct, and it has been right about that for 123 years.
sections.ethics: Onward Holdings, J. Press's Japanese parent since 1986, is one of Japan's largest apparel conglomerates, with manufacturing spread across Japan, China, Vietnam, and other production countries depending on the label. The U.S. line's domestically made products appear genuine, the brand merchandises origin clearly, but the parent company provides limited English-language detail on labor standards or supply chain auditing, and there is no meaningful public transparency at the factory level for the American products. There are no documented labor scandals specific to the J. Press U.S. operation; the concern is opacity rather than misconduct. We've reached out to J. Press for more detail on their labor practices and will update this section when we hear back.
sections.heritage: One hundred and twenty-three years is a long time to hold a single aesthetic conviction, and J. Press has largely held it. Jacobi Press founded the brand in New Haven in 1902, grew it through the Ivy League corridor over the following decades, and established an identity so coherent that the brand survived his family's departure intact. The 1974 licensing deal with Onward Kashiyama, the first American clothing brand ever licensed in Japan, turned out to be a preview: by 1986, Onward had bought the whole company. That transition could have meant drift. It largely hasn't. The American stores and website have continued to produce the Oxford shirt, the sack suit, and the Shaggy Dog in forms that would be recognizable to anyone who shopped there in 1955. Japanese ownership added a parallel creative universe in Japan without dismantling the original one in New Haven.
sections.value: Made-in-USA Oxford cloth button-downs run $125–135, which is a fair price for a domestically sewn shirt with no interlining, a soft collar that breaks in properly, and a construction standard that outlasts anything in its price category at the mall. For context, that's less than comparable shirts from the current Brooks Brothers lineup and considerably less than shirts from English makers like Turnbull & Asser, while offering genuine American manufacture. Shetland wool Shaggy Dog sweaters land in a similar range. Suits and sport coats climb higher, as tailored clothing does, but the construction quality earns it. J. Press runs a semi-annual clearance sale at the end of each selling season, late winter and late summer, when discounts on knitwear and tailoring can be meaningful. If you have a specific sweater color in mind and some patience, waiting for that window is a reasonable play.
